Gastrointestinal Disorders

Constipation

Constipation is a symptom complex, not a diagnosis. ED work is to separate functional constipation from obstruction, fecal impaction, medication/toxin effect, metabolic disease, neurologic disease, malignancy, perforation, and pseudo-obstruction.

Board trap: Diarrhea does not rule out constipation; liquid stool can leak around a fecal impaction or obstructing lesion.

CONSTIPATION

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Patients may mean infrequent stools, hard stool, straining, painful defecation, bloating, or incomplete evacuation. Chronic constipation generally persists for at least 3 months; acute new constipation, especially in older adults, deserves an organic-cause search.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Constipation arises from slow transit, outlet dysfunction, reduced intake or activity, medications, metabolic/electrolyte disorders, neurologic disease, psychiatric disease, anatomic lesions, and painful anorectal processes. The mechanism determines whether fiber helps, harms, or delays a needed obstruction workup.

CLINICAL FEATURES

HISTORY

Ask the patient to define constipation and clarify onset, stool caliber, flatus, vomiting, abdominal pain/distention, weight loss, fever, bleeding, anemia symptoms, rectal pain, prior abdominal surgery, cancer history, neurologic symptoms, diet, fluid intake, mobility, pregnancy, medications, opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, and laxative/enema use. New constipation after age 50, weight loss, blood, anemia, fever, vomiting, or obstipation is not routine functional constipation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Focused abdominal, pelvic, and rectal examinations look for hernia, mass, distention, bowel-sound pattern, peritoneal signs, fissure, hemorrhoid, abscess, prolapse, fecal impaction, obstructing rectal mass, occult/gross blood, and neurologic tone. Failure to perform a rectal exam is a common reason fecal impaction is missed.

LABORATORY EVALUATION AND IMAGING

Do not order routine labs for every uncomplicated constipation patient. Test when organic disease is suspected: CBC for anemia/infection, electrolytes including potassium, calcium, magnesium when indicated, thyroid testing for hypothyroid suspicion, and lead/iron or toxin testing when the history suggests it.

Plain radiographs can show stool burden, colonic/rectal dilation, and air-fluid levels, but CT is preferred for obstruction, perforation, mass, severe pain, concerning exam, or unclear diagnosis. Normal stool burden on x-ray does not exclude serious abdominal disease if the clinical picture is concerning.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

FUNCTIONAL CONSTIPATION

Functional constipation is managed with education, fluids, mobility, dietary fiber when appropriate, polyethylene glycol, lactulose, stimulants, suppositories, or enemas depending on stool location and patient risk. There is no single medication fix; reassessment and outpatient follow-up matter.

OPIOID-INDUCED BOWEL DYSFUNCTION

Opioids reduce peristalsis and secretion through gut mu-opioid receptors. Conventional laxatives may fail; peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists can help selected patients when obstruction is excluded. Do not use a PAMORA when bowel obstruction or perforation risk is present.

FECAL IMPACTION

Impaction requires disimpaction before discharge. Enemas alone may fail, especially with firm distal stool. Provide analgesia, consider sedation when needed, and then build a bowel regimen so the patient can maintain evacuation.

INTESTINAL PSEUDO-OBSTRUCTION (OGILVIE'S SYNDROME)

Ogilvie syndrome is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction with massive dilation but no mechanical blockage. It occurs in medically ill, postoperative, neurologically impaired, or immobilized patients. Progressive cecal/colonic dilation risks ischemia and perforation. Management may require decompression, neostigmine, colonoscopy, or surgery depending on severity and contraindications.

ORGANIC CONSTIPATION

Organic constipation is suggested by acute onset, obstruction symptoms, fever, vomiting, bleeding, anemia, weight loss, rectal pain, neurologic deficits, cancer risk, electrolyte disease, hypothyroidism, medication toxicity, or change in stool caliber. Treatment is the underlying diagnosis, not simply more laxatives.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Many patients can discharge after adequate evacuation plan, oral tolerance, pain control, and no red flags. Address obstruction, systemic illness, medication effect, electrolyte imbalance, and self-administered enema perforation risk before discharge. Hospitalize or consult surgery/GI when obstruction, perforation, severe pain, vomiting, fecal impaction not cleared, Ogilvie syndrome, stercoral colitis, or serious organic disease is suspected.
